name: Margin Check
question: What’s left from each sale?
scope: Up to 10 products, services or projects; one price-or-cost scenario; a one-page summary with up to three points to investigate.
problem: Three projects generated $50,000 in sales. How much is left after paying the costs of doing that work?
inputLabel: Sales and delivery costs for three fictional projects

inputs.note: Delivery costs are the costs assigned to doing these projects. Rent, other shared running costs, interest and tax are excluded.

metrics.label: Left after delivery costs
metrics.detail: Still has to cover rent, other running costs and tax.

metrics.label: Percentage of sales left
metrics.detail: $24 of every $100 sold remains after delivery costs.

finding: Three projects generated $50,000 in sales and cost $38,000 to deliver, leaving $12,000.
nextStep: Before setting the next price, check that every delivery cost is included and whether the amount left covers the remaining running costs.

qa.question: Does the $12,000 mean profit?
qa.answer: It is the amount left after the costs of doing these projects. Rent, other shared running costs, interest and tax still have to come out of it. You need those figures before you can calculate final profit.

qa.question: Which projects leave more?
qa.answer: Project A leaves $6,000 from $20,000 in sales: $30 per $100. Project B leaves $3,600 from $18,000, and Project C leaves $2,400 from $12,000: $20 per $100 each. Their prices and delivery costs need checking; these figures do not tell us why they differ.

qa.question: What should I check before the next quote?
qa.answer: Check that the estimate includes every cost of doing the work. Compare the price and cost breakdown for Projects B and C with Project A. In the extra-cost example below, another $5,000 of costs cuts the amount left from $12,000 to $7,000.

scenario.title: What if the same work costs $5,000 more?
scenario.description: Keep sales at $50,000. Increase delivery costs from $38,000 to $43,000. The amount left falls from $12,000 to $7,000.
scenario.note: Only delivery costs change in this example. Rent, other running costs and tax still have to be covered.

deliverables: A comparison of money left after delivery costs for the three projects
One cost-increase scenario
A one-page summary with up to three checks to make before the next quote
cautions: Delivery costs cover the costs assigned to doing the work. Rent, other shared running costs, interest and tax must still be paid.
The cost increase is an assumption to test. It is not a prediction.
calculationNotes: Left after delivery: $50,000 − $38,000 = $12,000. Divide $12,000 by $50,000 to get 24%, or $24 left per $100 sold.
Project A leaves $6,000 of $20,000, or $30 per $100 sold. Project B leaves $3,600 of $18,000, and Project C leaves $2,400 of $12,000: each leaves $20 per $100 sold.
With the extra cost: $50,000 − $43,000 = $7,000. Divide $7,000 by $50,000 to get 14%, or $14 left per $100 sold.
meaning: That is $24 per $100 sold, before rent, other running costs and tax.
takeaway: Check that the $24 left from every $100 sold covers your other running costs before setting your next price.

name: Four-Week Cash Snapshot
question: What if a customer pays late?
scope: Opening cash plus up to 20 dated expected receipts and payments; a four-week forecast; one delayed-payment scenario; a one-page summary.
problem: The business starts with $30,000. A customer is due to pay $40,000 on 16 November. What happens if that payment arrives on 26 November instead?
inputLabel: Starting cash: $30,000. Expected payments in and out: 2–29 November 2026

inputs.note: Fictional forecast for 2–29 November 2026. Payments happen on the listed dates. No overdraft or other borrowing is included.

metrics.label: Cash at the end if customers pay on time
Lowest balance if customers pay on time
Shortfall if the $40,000 payment is late

finding: A $40,000 customer payment arriving ten days late creates a $10,000 shortfall on 20 November.
nextStep: Confirm the customer’s payment date and how the $10,000 gap would be covered before the supplier bill is due.

qa.question: Why does a late payment matter if the month ends with $35,000?
qa.answer: On 20 November, a $25,000 supplier bill is due. Without the $40,000 customer payment, only $15,000 is available. The business needs another $10,000 that day, even though later payments bring the final balance back to $35,000.

qa.question: What does −$10,000 on the chart mean?
qa.answer: It means the listed bills exceed the cash available by $10,000 on 20 November. It is a funding gap to resolve, not an approved overdraft. The chart checks each payment date, so a positive final balance cannot hide an earlier gap.

qa.question: What should I check before the bill is due?
qa.answer: Confirm when the customer will pay and whether the supplier’s 20 November due date is fixed. Check any cash already available for the gap. If the payment date needs to change, agree that with the supplier in advance.

scenario.title: Same money, different payment date
scenario.description: Move only the $40,000 customer payment from 16 November to 26 November. All other dates and amounts stay the same.
scenario.note: The shortfall happens on 20 November, in week 3. The table shows week-end balances; the chart also checks every listed payment date. A negative figure is funding needed, not an agreed overdraft.

deliverables: A four-week cash forecast from the eight entries
One delayed-receipt scenario
A one-page summary of the potential gap and receipt/payment questions
cautions: The forecast depends on the listed amounts arriving or leaving on the stated dates.
A negative forecast shows money that would be needed. It does not mean the bank has agreed an overdraft.
Sales and profit are different from money received in the bank. Unlisted bills or taxes would change this forecast.
calculationNotes: Total customer payments expected: $30,000 + $20,000 + $40,000 + $25,000 = $115,000.
End-of-period balance: $30,000 starting cash + $115,000 received − $110,000 paid = $35,000.
With the late payment, $15,000 is available before the $25,000 supplier bill on 20 November. $15,000 − $25,000 = −$10,000, a $10,000 shortfall.
After that shortfall: −$10,000 + $25,000 received on 23 November + $40,000 received on 26 November − $20,000 paid on 27 November = $35,000.
meaning: The final $35,000 balance cannot pay a bill that was due earlier.
takeaway: Confirm payment dates early so a $10,000 cash gap does not leave a bill unpaid.

name: Plan vs Actual Review
question: Why did we miss the plan?
scope: An existing budget and matching actuals for up to three months and 15 categories; the three largest differences by value; a one-page summary.
problem: Over two months, the business expected to have $45,000 left after delivery costs, payroll and rent. It had $22,000 left. Where did the $23,000 difference come from?
inputLabel: Two months of planned and actual sales and costs

inputs.note: Only sales, delivery costs, payroll and rent are shown. Other costs, interest and tax are excluded. Use matching periods and categories for a fair comparison.

metrics.label: Planned amount left
metrics.detail: After the listed costs, over two months.

metrics.label: Actual amount left
metrics.detail: After the same cost categories, over two months.

finding: $22,000 is left after delivery costs, payroll and rent, against a $45,000 plan.
nextStep: Compare actual orders with the sales plan first, then check payroll records and supplier bills for the reasons.

qa.question: How does the $23,000 gap add up?
qa.answer: Sales were $15,000 below plan. Payroll was $6,000 above plan, and delivery costs were $2,000 above plan. All three reduce the amount left: $15,000 + $6,000 + $2,000 = $23,000. Rent matched the plan.

qa.question: Does this tell us why sales fell or costs rose?
qa.answer: No. It shows where the differences are. Compare actual orders with the sales plan, payroll records with the staffing plan, and supplier bills with the delivery-cost budget. Those records are needed to explain the changes.

qa.question: Which difference should I look at first?
qa.answer: Start with the $15,000 sales gap because it is the largest. Then investigate the $6,000 extra payroll and $2,000 extra delivery costs. Check whether each difference is temporary or should change the next budget.

scenario.title: The three changes behind the $23,000 gap
scenario.description: Add both months together. Lower sales and higher costs each reduce the amount left.
scenario.note: Rent was $20,000 both in the plan and in the actual results, so it adds nothing to the gap.

deliverables: A matching monthly plan-versus-actual comparison
The top three differences by value
A one-page summary with possible drivers and team questions
cautions: The comparison shows which numbers changed. It does not prove what caused the changes.
Only the listed costs are deducted. Other costs, interest and tax may reduce the amount left.
This is a comparison of sales and costs. It does not show when customers paid or bills left the bank.
calculationNotes: Planned amount left: $210,000 sales − $105,000 delivery costs − $40,000 payroll − $20,000 rent = $45,000.
Actual amount left: $195,000 sales − $107,000 delivery costs − $46,000 payroll − $20,000 rent = $22,000.
$15,000 less sales + $6,000 extra payroll + $2,000 extra delivery costs = $23,000 less left. Rent is unchanged.
The example uses two months and four categories, within the starter project limits.
meaning: $15,000 less sales, $6,000 extra payroll and $2,000 extra delivery costs explain the $23,000 gap.
takeaway: Check the sales shortfall first: it explains $15,000 of the $23,000 gap.

name: AI Finance Workflow Setup
question: Can AI help with our monthly update?
scope: One approved spreadsheet input to one draft commentary workflow in the client’s approved ChatGPT or Claude setup; reusable prompt, input template, sample draft, basic tests, human-review checklist and walkthrough.
problem: A business wants to turn its monthly spreadsheet into a short explanation without writing the update from scratch each time.
inputLabel: One example spreadsheet: planned and actual sales and costs

inputs.note: The sample draft is prewritten, not a live AI chat. Only the sales and costs listed here are included.

finding: The example draft summarises a $10,000 gap: $5,000 left after the listed costs, against a $15,000 plan.
nextStep: Test the approved template with known totals and missing numbers before using real drafts.
draftCommentary: Sales were $90,000 against a $100,000 plan: $10,000 lower. Delivery costs were $2,000 lower, but other running costs were $2,000 higher, so the total cost was unchanged. That left $5,000 after the listed costs, instead of $15,000. Compare actual orders with the sales plan to find the reason; these figures alone do not explain it.

qa.question: What does the workflow actually do?
qa.answer: You put the agreed monthly figures into a spreadsheet template. Reusable instructions ask the approved AI tool to draft a short explanation of the differences. A person then checks and edits it. This page illustrates that process with a prewritten draft.

qa.question: What should the draft say about these figures?
qa.answer: Sales were $10,000 below plan. Delivery costs were $2,000 lower and other running costs $2,000 higher, leaving total costs unchanged. The amount left therefore fell from the planned $15,000 to $5,000. The draft should ask for the reason for lower sales, rather than make one up.

qa.question: How do we check that the workflow is useful?
qa.answer: Test it with these known totals, then with a missing number, text in a number field and an unsupported explanation. It should flag problems rather than fill gaps by guessing. A person must still check the input, calculations and wording before each draft is used.

scenario.title: Four checks before using a draft
scenario.description: These are test cases and expected responses for the proposed workflow. This web page does not run the tests.

rows.expected: Calculate $15,000 planned and $5,000 actual left after the listed costs, with a $10,000 gap.

rows.test: A required actual amount is blank
rows.expected: Ask for the missing number. Do not treat the blank as zero.
Flag the invalid entry and stop the numerical explanation until it is corrected.

rows.test: A note gives a reason without evidence
rows.expected: Mark the reason as unverified or ask for supporting information. Do not state it as a fact.

scenario.note: Passing these basic tests does not guarantee every future draft will be correct. Human checking remains necessary.

deliverables: A reusable prompt and one input template
A sample draft and simple checks to test it
A human-review checklist and walkthrough
cautions: A person must check every real AI draft before it is shared or used for a financial decision.
Use only data and tools approved for this purpose. This demonstration uses fictional figures.
Tool subscriptions, API charges, custom connections and ongoing support are separate.
Any Excel add-in depends on compatibility and administrator approval.
calculationNotes: Planned amount left: $100,000 sales − $60,000 delivery costs − $25,000 other running costs = $15,000.
Actual amount left: $90,000 sales − $58,000 delivery costs − $27,000 other running costs = $5,000.
Both planned and actual costs total $85,000. The $10,000 fall in sales therefore explains the $10,000 gap in the amount left.
The displayed draft is stored example text. The page does not call an AI model.
meaning: AI can draft an update, but a person must check it. This is a prewritten illustration.
takeaway: Let AI draft the update, then have a person check the figures and explanations.

name: Plan a hire or expansion
question: Will extra sales cover a new hire?
scope: Illustrative tailored planning work. The actual budget, forecast, scenarios, deliverables, timeline and fee are agreed separately after discussing the decision.
problem: The example hire costs $30,000 a month, plus $20,000 to set up. The business expects each extra $100 of sales to leave $50 after delivery costs.
inputLabel: Three monthly cases: no hire, expected sales and lower sales

inputs.note: Assume $60,000 starting cash, delivery costs of $50 per $100 sold, and existing fixed costs of $70,000 a month. All sales are collected and all monthly costs are paid in the same month. The $30,000 hire cost includes the employment costs assumed in this example. Setup cash is separate.

metrics.label: Extra monthly sales to cover hire
metrics.detail: Assumes $50 of each extra $100 sold is left after delivery costs.

metrics.label: One-time setup payment
metrics.detail: Separate from the monthly hire cost.

metrics.label: First month-end cash with expected sales
metrics.detail: Assumes all sales are collected in the same month.

finding: A $30,000 monthly hire needs $60,000 more monthly sales, assuming half of each sale is left after delivery.
nextStep: Check how quickly those sales and customer payments could arrive, and whether cash covers the wait.

qa.question: Why does a $30,000 hire need $60,000 more sales?
qa.answer: Half of every extra sale pays for delivery in this example. Another $60,000 in sales leaves $30,000 after delivery, which then pays the hire’s $30,000 monthly cost. The amount left after monthly costs stays at $30,000, the same as without the hire.

qa.question: What if the hire brings only $20,000 more sales?
qa.answer: Only $10,000 of that extra sales amount remains after delivery costs. The hire still costs $30,000, so the business has $20,000 less left than without the hire: $10,000 instead of $30,000 after monthly costs.

qa.question: Can the business afford the setup and the wait for sales?
qa.answer: That needs a cash forecast. This example starts with $60,000 and assumes immediate customer payment. After the $20,000 setup payment, first month-end cash is $70,000 with expected sales or $50,000 with lower sales. Check the full hire cost, payment dates and a slower start before deciding.

scenario.title: How much is left, and what happens to first-month cash?
scenario.description: Each case starts with $60,000 cash. First add the amount left after monthly costs, then subtract the one-time setup payment where there is a hire.
scenario.note: Monthly results exclude the one-time setup payment, unlisted costs, interest and tax. The cash figures assume all sales and monthly costs are received or paid in that month.

deliverables: An agreed budget or scenario model around the hiring decision
A comparison of recurring costs, one-time cash needs and assumptions
A walkthrough of the trade-offs and information still needed
cautions: Expected extra sales are assumptions, not guaranteed results.
The $60,000 figure only covers the assumed monthly hire cost at the stated delivery-cost rate. It does not recover the setup payment.
This is a simplified example of a tailored project. Scope, deliverables, timing and fees are agreed separately.
calculationNotes: The assumption is that half of sales remains after delivery costs: ($200,000 − $100,000) ÷ $200,000 = 50%.
Extra monthly sales needed to cover the hire: $30,000 ÷ 50% = $60,000.
No hire: $200,000 sales − $100,000 delivery costs − $70,000 existing fixed costs = $30,000 left.
Hire with expected sales: $260,000 − $130,000 − $70,000 − $30,000 = $30,000 left after monthly costs.
Hire with lower sales: $220,000 − $110,000 − $70,000 − $30,000 = $10,000 left after monthly costs.

Starting with $60,000 cash, expected first-month closing cash is $60,000 + $30,000 − $20,000 setup = $70,000. With lower sales it is $60,000 + $10,000 − $20,000 = $50,000. Without a hire it is $60,000 + $30,000 = $90,000.
meaning: That only covers the monthly hire cost; the $20,000 setup payment is extra.
takeaway: Check whether $60,000 in extra monthly sales is realistic before committing to the hire.

name: Understand cash and profit
question: We made a profit. Where’s the cash?
scope: Illustrative deeper review of pricing, margins or cash flow. The area to investigate, deliverables, timeline and fee are agreed separately.
problem: For one month, the listed sales and costs show $30,000 profit. Yet the bank balance falls from $50,000 to $35,000. The difference comes from when money was received or paid.
inputLabel: One fictional month: sales, costs and actual payments

rows.item: Additional unsold stock bought and paid for

inputs.note: The example has no customer or supplier balances carried over from an earlier month. The $20,000 extra stock is still unsold, so it is separate from the $60,000 cost of items sold. No other cash movements, depreciation, interest or tax are included.

metrics.label: Profit from the listed sales and costs
metrics.detail: Other costs, depreciation, interest and tax are excluded.

finding: $30,000 profit is shown, yet the bank balance falls from $50,000 to $35,000.
nextStep: Confirm customer payment dates, review unsold stock and plan for those supplier bills.

qa.question: Why is profit different from money in the bank?
qa.answer: The accounts include $120,000 of sales, but customers have paid only $80,000. The business also paid $20,000 for stock it has not sold yet. Sales can count before payment arrives, and buying unsold stock can use cash before its cost appears in profit.

qa.question: Why does the chart add $15,000 of unpaid supplier bills?
qa.answer: Profit already deducts $60,000 for the items sold, but only $45,000 has been paid to suppliers. Add back the unpaid $15,000 when explaining the cash change because that money has not left the bank yet. It is still owed; it is not extra income.

qa.question: How does the full cash calculation work?
qa.answer: Start with the $30,000 listed profit. Subtract $40,000 of sales not yet collected, add $15,000 of supplier costs not yet paid, then subtract $20,000 spent on extra stock. The result is a $15,000 cash decrease. Check the unpaid invoices and supplier due dates, and whether the extra stock is needed.

scenario.title: How $30,000 profit becomes a $15,000 cash decrease
scenario.description: Adjust the listed profit for sales not yet paid, supplier costs not yet paid and stock bought but not yet sold.

rows.item: Start with profit from the listed items
Subtract sales customers have not paid
Add back supplier costs not yet paid
Subtract extra unsold stock paid for

scenario.note: Starting cash $50,000 minus the $15,000 cash decrease leaves $35,000. The $15,000 unpaid supplier bills must still be paid later.

deliverables: An agreed review of the relevant profit and cash drivers
A clear reconciliation or model using the agreed data
A walkthrough of the findings and next questions
cautions: The $30,000 profit is based only on the listed sales and costs. Other costs, depreciation, interest and tax are excluded.
A real business may need more adjustments than this simplified example.
Tailored scope, deliverables, timing and fees are agreed separately.
calculationNotes: Profit from the listed items: $120,000 sales − $60,000 cost of items sold − $30,000 other costs = $30,000.
Customers have not yet paid $120,000 − $80,000 = $40,000 of sales.
The business has not yet paid $60,000 − $45,000 = $15,000 of supplier costs already included in profit.
Convert the listed profit to the cash change: $30,000 − $40,000 uncollected sales + $15,000 unpaid supplier costs − $20,000 extra stock = −$15,000.
Check using actual payments: $80,000 received − $45,000 supplier payments − $30,000 other payments − $20,000 extra stock = −$15,000.
Cash at month-end: $50,000 starting balance − $15,000 decrease = $35,000.
meaning: Customers still owe $40,000; extra stock used $20,000. Unpaid supplier bills kept $15,000 in the bank for now.
takeaway: Follow up unpaid customer invoices and review stock purchases before assuming profit is available to spend.

name: Assess marketing performance
question: Are our ads paying their way?
scope: Analysis of existing marketing spend, sales and customer-profitability data, with assumptions and gaps made clear. Tailored scope and fee are agreed separately.
problem: Social ads cost less per new customer than Search ads. The comparison checks whether those customers’ first orders cover both delivery and advertising costs.
inputLabel: First orders from new customers recorded against two ad channels

inputs.note: Assume 60 different new paying customers, each counted once and linked to one channel in the supplied records. Sales are after discounts and refunds. Delivery costs include fulfilling the orders. Later purchases, shared running costs, interest and tax are excluded.

metrics.label: Search: left after delivery and ads
metrics.detail: Before shared running costs and tax.

metrics.label: Social: left after delivery and ads
metrics.detail: A negative value means first orders did not cover these costs.

metrics.label: Search: ad cost per new customer
Social: ad cost per new customer

finding: Search orders leave $6,000 after delivery and ads. Social orders fall $800 short of those costs.
nextStep: Check sales, refunds and delivery costs for each channel, then compare repeat purchases before changing spend.

qa.question: Why does Search look better even though its customers cost more?
qa.answer: Per new customer, Search has $2,000 in first-order sales, $1,200 in delivery costs and $500 in ads, leaving $300. Social has $600 in sales, $420 in delivery costs and $200 in ads, leaving a $20 shortfall. These are averages from the example records.

qa.question: Does −$800 mean Social had negative sales?
qa.answer: No. Social generated $24,000 in sales. Delivery cost $16,800 and ads cost $8,000, for total costs of $24,800. The −$800 is the shortfall after those costs. It is not sales revenue or a sales-to-ad-spend ratio.

qa.question: Should we move the budget to Search?
qa.answer: These figures alone do not settle that. First check that customers are counted once, sales are assigned consistently, and refunds and delivery costs are complete. Then compare later purchases and any other relevant costs. The example only covers first orders and does not prove which sales the ads caused.

scenario.title: What one new customer leaves, on average
scenario.description: Divide each channel’s first-order sales, delivery costs and ad spend by its number of new customers.
scenario.note: The after-ad result already deducts delivery costs. It is not total sales or a sales-to-ad-spend ratio. Matching a sale to a channel does not prove the ad caused it.

deliverables: A performance analysis using existing spend, sales and cost records
Clearly defined measures, assumptions and evidence gaps
Questions and options to review before taking action
cautions: The analysis covers marketing results. It does not include running campaigns, SEO or producing content.
Only first purchases are included. Later purchases, shared running costs, interest and tax are excluded.
A sale recorded against a channel is not proof that the advertisement caused it.
Tailored scope, deliverables, timing and fees are agreed separately.
calculationNotes: Search: $40,000 sales − $24,000 delivery costs − $10,000 ads = $6,000 left.
Social: $24,000 sales − $16,800 delivery costs − $8,000 ads = −$800. Costs exceed first-order sales by $800.
Search ad cost per new customer: $10,000 ÷ 20 = $500. Social: $8,000 ÷ 40 = $200.
Search average left per customer: $2,000 sales − $1,200 delivery costs − $500 ads = $300. Across 20 customers, that is $6,000.
Social average left per customer: $600 sales − $420 delivery costs − $200 ads = −$20. Across 40 customers, that is −$800.
Both channels combined: $64,000 sales − $40,800 delivery costs − $18,000 ads = $5,200 left before shared running costs and tax.
meaning: Social’s ad cost per new customer is lower, but their first orders leave less to cover that cost.
takeaway: Compare what each channel leaves after delivery and ads, then check repeat purchases before changing spend.

name: Make reporting more useful
question: Sales are up. Is the business healthier?
scope: An agreed reporting pack, performance dashboard or defined spreadsheet workflow, with documentation and a team handover. Tailored scope and fee are agreed separately.
problem: The monthly report shows higher sales. It also needs to show how much each sale leaves and which customer payments are late, so the team knows what to check.
inputLabel: Two months compared using the same definitions

rows.item: Customer invoices past their payment due date

inputs.note: The same definitions are used in both months. Overdue invoices are customer bills past their payment due date. Overdue invoices and cash are measured at month-end. The review levels below are choices for this fictional business.

metrics.label: Percentage of sales left after delivery
metrics.detail: $35 per $100 sold, down from $40. Shared running costs and tax are not deducted.

finding: Sales rose $20,000, but each $100 sold leaves $35 after delivery, down from $40. Overdue customer payments rose from $10,000 to $25,000.
nextStep: Ask sales and operations to check prices and costs. Ask finance to confirm overdue invoice payment dates.

qa.question: Did the business make more from its sales?
qa.answer: The total left after delivery rose from $40,000 to $42,000, so there was $2,000 more. But sales rose by $20,000. Each $100 sold now leaves $35 instead of $40 because delivery costs rose faster than sales. Shared running costs and tax still have to be covered.

qa.question: Do overdue payments explain the lower bank balance?
qa.answer: Not on their own. Overdue invoices rose from $10,000 to $25,000, while cash fell from $40,000 to $35,000. Check actual customer receipts and all other payments to explain the cash movement. The report does not show enough detail to establish the cause.

qa.question: How should the team use this report?
qa.answer: Ask sales and operations to compare prices and delivery costs between the months. Ask finance to list the overdue invoices, confirm expected payment dates and check upcoming bills. Agree when those checks will be reviewed, so the report leads to specific follow-up work.

scenario.title: Which result needs a check, and who will do it?
scenario.description: For this fictional business, the team has chosen the review levels below. They are starting points for a check, not universal targets.

rows.measure: Percentage of sales left after delivery
rows.question: Compare prices and delivery costs with last month. Which products or jobs changed?
List overdue invoices, confirm payment dates and follow up unpaid amounts.
The balance is above this level. Still compare upcoming bills with dated expected receipts.

scenario.note: Being above the $30,000 cash review level does not show that every upcoming bill can be paid. Check the dated cash forecast as well.

deliverables: An agreed reporting pack, dashboard or spreadsheet workflow
Definitions, update instructions and validation checks
A handover so the team can own the reporting process
cautions: The amount left after delivery costs still needs to cover shared running costs, interest and tax.
The sample is a static report. It is not connected to live business records.
The example review levels are choices for this fictional business, not industry standards or guarantees of safety.
Tailored scope, deliverables, timing and fees are agreed separately.
calculationNotes: Previous amount left after delivery: $100,000 − $60,000 = $40,000, or $40 per $100 sold.
Current amount left after delivery: $120,000 − $78,000 = $42,000, or $35 per $100 sold.
Sales increased by $20,000. Divide $20,000 by $100,000 to get 20%.
Delivery costs increased by $18,000. Divide $18,000 by $60,000 to get 30%.
The amount left increased by $2,000. Divide $2,000 by $40,000 to get 5%.
The percentage of sales left fell from 40% to 35%, a fall of 5 percentage points.
Overdue payments rose by $25,000 − $10,000 = $15,000. Cash fell by $40,000 − $35,000 = $5,000. These totals do not explain all the movements in cash.
meaning: Despite higher sales, only $2,000 more is left after delivery. More customer money is also past due.
takeaway: Look beyond sales: check shrinking margins and follow up overdue customer payments.
